name: Sam Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No problem. I'll try to be straight with you.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a business insurer, in a small office above a bank on the high street. I handle the paperwork for small firms: cafés, builders, a couple of taxi companies, a dog groomer. They ring when they add a van or hire someone, and I update the policy, issue the certificates and chase the ones who haven't paid. Builders always need a certificate by tomorrow morning for some site, so the afternoons are a scramble.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the regulars. There's a café owner, Mrs Okafor, who rings every month to check she's covered for something new, and she always asks about my mum. What wears me out is the chasing, and the pay, which hasn't kept up with anything. I live with my girlfriend Ama, who's a receptionist at a dental surgery. We're saving for a wedding, but honestly we've got about three weeks of money and the wedding fund is mostly an idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I think that's possible, honestly. A lot of what I've seen is hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. I've used the tools a bit, they're handy for summing up long policy wording, but they get things wrong. I'd say at work that we should use them for the boring bits and keep the people for the customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, even the boring bits are a big chunk of my day. Issuing certificates is routine, so if the system does that automatically, they might not need three of us in the office. Probably they'd keep us, because the customers like a person, but my pay still wouldn't go anywhere. And the wedding would keep getting pushed back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, use the tools a little more where they actually save time, and ask my manager about the account handler role, which pays a bit more. I'd also set up a standing order of forty a month into the wedding pot, even if it's small. And I'd keep an eye on the bank downstairs, because if they close, the rent on our office goes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just stuck. It's a feeling of running to stand still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the account handler role involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You look after a set of business customers, visit them once a year, and work out what cover they actually need. It's more talking, less typing. The person who has it now, Gary, retires next year, so I'd put my hand up early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ama say about the wedding being pushed back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say fine, but her mum wouldn't. Ama's mum has been asking about a date since we moved in together. I'd tell Ama (my girlfriend) we'll marry when we can pay for it ourselves, not on a credit card.

say: AI tools are **handy** for summing up policy wording but still get things wrong.
Use AI for **the boring bits** and keep people for the customers.
think: Issuing certificates is **routine**, so the office might not need three people.
His pay would stay flat and the **wedding** would keep slipping.
do: Use the tools a little more where they **save time**.
Ask about the **account handler role** before Gary retires.
Set up **forty a month** into the wedding pot.
feel: **Uneasy** and stuck, like running to stand still.
S0.quote: I'd tell Ama (my girlfriend) we'll marry when we can pay for it ourselves, not on a credit card.
fieldNote: Sam sees AI as **useful but limited**, from his own use.
His real pressure is **flat pay** and a delayed wedding.
He spots the **account handler role** as a way to move toward people work.
He's pragmatic: small, **steady steps** rather than big moves.

steps.text: Use the AI tool to sum up long policy wording
Apply for Gary's account handler role before he retires
Set up forty a month into the wedding pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Booking, checking, answering customers. That's a lot of my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to change, but companies should do it gradually and keep people who know the customers. I'd say it to my manager and anyone at the pub. Online, I'd probably share something balanced, not angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the certificate and admin part of my job goes. If customers can update their own van details through an app and the AI issues the certificate, there's not much left. If I get the account handler role, I might be okay, because business owners still want someone to talk to. If I don't, I'm in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard for the account handler job and learn the new systems properly once I see others using them. I'd ask Mrs Okafor and a couple of other regulars to put in a word with my manager. I'd also look at my cousin Kofi's removals firm as a backup, because lifting sofas isn't going to be done by a chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's not hopeless, but there are a lot of ifs, and our money is thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really ask a customer to put in a word for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, why not? Mrs Okafor (a café owner I look after) has been with us twelve years and she's already said she'd leave if she had to talk to a robot. A word from her is worth more than my appraisal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the wedding in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd push it back another year. We'd still get engaged properly, but a small one, family only. Ama would be fine with that, I think. Her mum less so.

say: Change makes sense, but firms should keep people who **know the customers**.
He'd share **balanced views** online rather than angry ones.
think: The **certificate work** goes once customers update details through an app.
Without the **account handler role**, he's in trouble.
do: Push hard for the **account handler** job.
Ask loyal customers like **Mrs Okafor** to speak up for him.
Keep his cousin Kofi's **removals firm** as a hands-on backup.
S1.quote: Mrs Okafor (a café owner I look after) has been with us twelve years and she's already said she'd leave if she had to talk to a robot.
fieldNote: Sam's survival depends on the **account handler role**.
He uses **customer loyalty** as a bargaining chip.
His backup is **hands-on work** through family.
The wedding gets **pushed back again**.

steps.text: Push for the account handler role with customer backing
Learn the new policy system once colleagues use it
Delay the wedding a year and plan a small family engagement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. That's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government to step in, but in a sensible way. Help for people who lose jobs, and make companies give notice. I wouldn't be on a march, but I'd vote for whoever had a real plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think even the account handler job goes. If AI can understand a business as well as a person, it can advise them too. The only thing left would be hands-on work, and that gives me until about 2031. So I'd be thinking about Kofi's removals firm seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Kofi for weekend work straight away, to learn the trade while I still have my job. I'd stop the wedding pot and put everything into rent savings. I'd also look at a van licence, because Kofi needs drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually the calm one, but two years doesn't leave room for calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ama?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're going to be okay, but we'd have to be careful. She'd probably ask if her job is safe, and I'd have to say I don't know. Receptionists are thinking work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robots coming later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the scary bit. Kofi's business would change too. Removals is hands-on work, but if robots can carry a sofa by 2031, I'd be buying time, not a future.

say: Government should step in **sensibly** to help people who lose jobs.
He'd **vote** for whoever had a real plan, rather than march.
think: Even the **account handler** job goes if AI can advise businesses.
do: Ask Kofi for **weekend removals work** straight away.
Stop the wedding pot and put everything into **rent savings**.
Get a **van licence** so he can drive for Kofi.
feel: **Alarmed**, though he's usually the calm one.
Aware he'd be **buying time**, not a future.
S2.quote: Removals is hands-on work, but if robots can carry a sofa by 2031, I'd be buying time, not a future.
fieldNote: Sam expects his **desk work to vanish** quickly.
He'd move into his cousin's **removals firm** to gain time.
He worries about **Ama's job** too, since it's also thinking work.
He's **pragmatic**, not ideological, about what government should do.

steps.text: Take weekend shifts at Kofi's removals firm
Move the wedding savings into rent savings
Vote for the party with a real plan for displaced workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's still fast, but it's some breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the five years should be used to train people and plan, not to argue. I'd tell my friends to start learning something practical now. Online I'd keep it calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd keep the account handler job until around 2030, maybe a bit longer if customers like me. Then I'd move into removals or something hands-on. That would last until about 2034, and maybe Kofi could buy robots and I'd help run them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the account handler role in the first year and start weekend removals with Kofi in the second year. I'd get the van licence early. We'd do a small wedding in two years instead of a big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it feels like there's a path. I can see a few steps ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned helping run robots. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my cousin Kofi's firm buys robots to carry stuff, someone still has to plan the jobs and deal with customers. I'm good with customers, so maybe I'd be the one who books the jobs and keeps the robots busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first to save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, definitely. And probably the gym. Ama would want to keep her yoga, so we'd cut my stuff first.

say: The five years should go on **training people** and planning, not arguing.
He'd tell friends to start learning **something practical** now.
think: He'd keep the **account handler** job until around 2030.
**Removals** work could last until 2034, maybe longer if he helps run robots.
do: Go for the **account handler** role in year one.
Start **weekend removals** and get a van licence early.
Plan a **small wedding** in two years.
feel: Able to see **a few steps** ahead.
S3.quote: If my cousin Kofi's firm buys robots to carry stuff, someone still has to plan the jobs and deal with customers.
fieldNote: Sam sees himself as the **customer-facing** link in any business.
Five years lets him **stack** jobs before switching.
He'd scale down to a **small wedding**.
His plan relies on **Kofi (his cousin)**.

steps.text: Apply for the account handler role this year
Get a van licence in the first year
Plan a small wedding in two years
Cut eating out and his gym membership

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that's a different story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for most people to change, but only if they start early. I'd tell people not to wait. I'd keep posting balanced stuff, maybe a bit more positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd keep the account handler job until 2033 or so. Then I'd move into Kofi's removals business, or maybe a property maintenance firm. That would last until about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the account handler role, save properly for the wedding, and do a weekend course in basic maintenance, like plumbing or tiling. We'd get married in three years. I'd keep using AI tools at work where they help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, because money's tight, but it's a manageable anxious. Ten years gives me room to do things in the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why maintenance rather than removals?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maintenance is more skilled and pays better. Removals is good work, but it's hard on your back by forty. With ten years, I'd want something I can do for longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future kids about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn with their hands and their heads. Don't rely on one kind of work. And be nice to customers, because people remember that.

say: Ten years is enough for most people to change if they **start early**.
He'd post **balanced** and slightly more positive views.
think: He'd keep the account handler job until **2033 or so**.
**Maintenance** or removals work would last until about 2039.
do: Get the **account handler** role and save for the wedding.
Take a weekend **maintenance course** in plumbing or tiling.
Use **AI tools** at work where they help.
feel: Glad to do things **in the right order**.
S4.quote: Removals is good work, but it's hard on your back by forty.
fieldNote: With ten years, Sam aims for **skilled hands-on work**.
He still feels **money pressure** from a thin cushion.
He thinks about **future kids** and lasting skills.
He'd keep using AI **pragmatically** at work.

steps.text: Do a weekend plumbing or tiling course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years is too fast for anyone with no savings. What would help is notice from employers and some kind of support while you retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about relationships. Mrs Okafor (a café owner I look after) will stay with us because she knows me, not because of the price. People forget that.

headlineQuote: Mrs Okafor (a café owner I look after) will stay with us because she knows me, not because of the price.
portrait: Sam is a **27-year-old business insurance clerk** who issues certificates for small firms.
He and Ama, a **dental receptionist**, have about three weeks of savings and a stalled wedding.
He's **pragmatic** and uses AI tools now and then for summaries.
His plan is the **account handler role**, then hands-on work through his cousin Kofi.
He values **customer relationships** as his edge.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too fast without savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice from employers** and support while retraining.
